questions.passage: The essay's ostensible subject is the migration of the Arctic tern, but its real business is methodological. By dwelling on how little the early ornithologists could actually observe—and how much they inferred from scraps—the author means to unsettle our confidence in any natural history built, as most are, on fragments. The tern is less the topic than the test case.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the migratory route of the Arctic tern in greater detail than the early ornithologists could.
To use the study of the Arctic tern's migration as a way of raising doubts about the evidentiary basis of natural history in general.
To defend the early ornithologists against the charge that their methods were unscientific.
To compare the Arctic tern's migration with that of other long-distance migratory birds.

questions.passage: The received wisdom treats boredom as mere absence—the empty space left when stimulation is withdrawn. A growing body of work reverses the picture. In this research, boredom is an active signal, a kind of alarm that fires when an activity has stopped yielding useful information, nudging the mind to seek a more rewarding task. Far from a void, boredom may be one of attention's most sophisticated instruments.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It defines a psychological state, lists its several causes, and then explains how it can be avoided.
It presents two competing theories and argues that both of them are mistaken.
It states a conventional view, notes that recent work reverses it, and then presents the alternative that replaces it.
It describes a discovery, traces its history, and then predicts its practical applications.

questions.passage: The standard history credits a single 1928 paper with founding the field. But that paper went almost entirely uncited for a decade, and its author later said she had regarded it at the time as a minor aside. Only in the 1940s, when unrelated work made its central idea suddenly useful, was the paper retrieved and its priority asserted—by others, and largely after the fact.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides biographical background explaining why the 1928 paper proved so immediately influential.
It concedes a minor objection before the text goes on to reaffirm the standard history.
It offers evidence that unsettles the standard history stated in the first sentence, which the rest of the text goes on to revise.
It illustrates the central idea that the 1928 paper is credited with having founded.

questions.passage: Conventional wisdom holds that specialists outperform generalists, and in stable fields they usually do. But when the rules of a field shift abruptly, the specialist's hard-won expertise can become a liability—a set of reflexes finely tuned to a world that no longer exists—while the generalist, having committed less deeply to any single approach, adapts more readily. Expertise, in other words, is not a fixed asset but one whose value depends on how much the world stays put.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Generalists reliably outperform specialists across nearly every field of endeavor.
The advantage of specialized expertise over broad, flexible knowledge depends on how stable the field in question remains.
Specialists are simply unable to adapt when the conditions of their field change.
Deep expertise is in all circumstances more valuable than a broad but shallow range of skills.

questions.passage: Mr. Calloway looked long at the canvas, and Idris watched him look. He had painted the face exactly as he found it—the softness about the mouth that the sitter took such pains to hide, the eyes forever calculating a sum. He had expected anger, perhaps a refusal to pay. What he had not expected was that Calloway would gaze at the portrait with the frank, delighted interest of a man meeting, for the first time, a stranger he found rather admirable.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Idris has deliberately flattered Calloway in the portrait in order to be certain of his payment.
Calloway fails to recognize, in the unflattering portrait, the revealing likeness of himself that Idris has captured.
Calloway is offended by the liberties that Idris has taken with his appearance.
Idris comes to regret having painted Calloway as harshly and exactly as he did.

questions.passage: Unlike most spiders, which detect prey by the vibrations of a web, the net-casting spider hunts by sight, and it does so in near-total darkness. Its enormous rear eyes are so light-sensitive that daylight would damage them; each night the spider manufactures a fresh layer of light-absorbing pigment within them and then destroys that layer again at dawn. The adaptation lets the animal see in conditions a tenth as bright as those the keenest cats require.
questions.question: According to the text, how does the net-casting spider keep daylight from damaging its eyes?
options: It hunts only on nights when little or no moonlight is present.
It relies on the vibrations of a web rather than on vision during the daylight hours.
It produces a layer of light-absorbing pigment in the eyes each night and breaks that layer down again at dawn.
It shelters its enormous rear eyes beneath a protective covering of web.

questions.passage: A historian argues that seventeenth-century London's coffeehouses functioned as the era's most important engines of commercial information, outpacing even printed newsletters in the speed with which they spread market-moving news.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
options: Coffeehouses of the period were often so crowded and noisy that sustained conversation among patrons was difficult.
Printed newsletters of the period reached a far larger total readership than any single coffeehouse could hold at one time.
Merchants of the period routinely learned of ship arrivals and price changes days earlier at their regular coffeehouse than in any printed newsletter.
Many coffeehouse patrons visited chiefly in order to read the newspapers that the establishments provided.

questions.passage: The novelist Wren Ashby is praised for conveying a character's social class not by describing it but through the objects the character happens to notice. A critic illustrating this technique might quote the sentence in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Ashby's fiction most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “He had grown up poor, and the memory of that poverty never left him for very long.”
“The drawing room was large and handsomely furnished, with tall windows overlooking the park.”
“Shown into the drawing room, he saw at once that the silver was plate, not sterling, and that the fire had been laid with yesterday's cinders.”
“She wondered whether he had ever, in the whole course of his life, wanted for anything at all.”

questions.passage: Researchers found that residents of a remote valley live unusually long, and they proposed that a mineral compound unusually abundant in the local spring water is responsible for that longevity.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the researchers' proposal?
options: Valley residents who moved away in youth and never drank the water as adults live, on average, just as long as those who remained.
The mineral compound abundant in the water has been shown, in laboratory studies, to slow the aging of cells.
The valley's residents also eat a diet rich in vegetables and perform hard physical labor well into old age.
Neighboring valleys, whose spring water lacks the compound, show only ordinary life expectancies.

questions.passage: An astronomer proposes that a certain star's periodic dimming is caused not by an orbiting planet but by a vast cloud of dust and debris circling the star. On this hypothesis, the dimming should differ in a way that a solid, opaque planet could not produce.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the astronomer's hypothesis?
options: The dimming recurs at almost perfectly regular intervals, precisely as the orbit of a planet would predict.
The star is among the very brightest objects in its region of the night sky.
Several other stars in the same cluster show no periodic dimming of any kind.
The star dims more at red wavelengths than at blue ones—the pattern expected when starlight passes through dust, but not when a solid body blocks it.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Two bridges of the same length were built across the same river.
  • Bridge X, a suspension design, cost $210 million and took 4 years to build.
  • Bridge Y, a cantilever design, cost $340 million and took 7 years to build.
  • Both bridges carry the same number of traffic lanes.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the difference in cost between the two bridges. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Bridge X, a suspension design, and Bridge Y, a cantilever design, were both built across the same river.
Though the two bridges span the same river and carry the same number of lanes, the cantilever Bridge Y cost $340 million—$130 million more than the suspension Bridge X.
Bridge Y, a cantilever design, cost $340 million and took 7 years to build.
Both of the bridges carry the same number of traffic lanes across the river.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Rosetta Stone (Egypt) records the same decree in three scripts.
  • The Behistun Inscription (Persia) records the same text in three languages.
  • In each case, a known script or language let scholars decode an unknown one.
  • The Rosetta Stone was key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs.
  • The Behistun Inscription was key to deciphering cuneiform.
questions.question: The student wants to make a generalization about the two inscriptions that is supported by the notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In both cases, a text repeated in a known script alongside an unknown one gave scholars the key that unlocked a previously unreadable writing system.
The Rosetta Stone records a single decree written out in three different scripts.
The Behistun Inscription proved crucial to the eventual decipherment of cuneiform.
Ancient scribes often recorded their most important texts in more than one language.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Lin Ostrom hypothesized that, among alpine plant species, those growing at higher elevations tend to be shorter.
  • Species A grows at 1,200 m; average height 40 cm.
  • Species B grows at 2,900 m; average height 9 cm.
  • Species C grows at 2,000 m; average height 22 cm.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Ostrom's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Species C grows at an elevation of 2,000 m and has an average height of 22 cm.
All three of the species are alpine plants adapted to life in mountain environments.
The species growing at the highest elevation, B (2,900 m), was the shortest (9 cm), while the species growing at the lowest elevation, A (1,200 m), was the tallest (40 cm).
Species B grows at a higher elevation than both Species A and Species C.

questions.passage: The paper's tables and regressions might suggest a narrowly empirical aim, but its purpose is polemical. Each statistic is marshaled to embarrass a single, once-dominant theory of urban growth—to show, number by number, that the theory predicts the opposite of what the cities actually did. The data are not the point; the demolition is.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To propose a new statistical method for measuring the growth of cities over time.
To defend a once-dominant theory of urban growth against its empirical critics.
To use empirical data primarily as a means of discrediting a formerly dominant theory of urban growth.
To compare the growth patterns of several different cities over the same period.

questions.passage: It is natural to assume that a language with more words can express more. The assumption dissolves on inspection. Where one language uses a single word, another uses a phrase; where one draws a fine distinction with vocabulary, another draws it with grammar or tone. What looks like a poverty of vocabulary is often only a different distribution of the same expressive labor across a language's other resources.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It defines a linguistic term and then traces how the term's meaning has changed over time.
It compares two particular languages and argues that one of them is more expressive.
It poses a question about language and then declines, in the end, to answer it.
It presents an intuitive assumption, asserts that scrutiny undoes it, and then explains why the assumption misleads.

questions.passage: By the 1800s, the guild's elaborate initiation rites were widely mocked as empty theater. Yet the very uselessness of the rites was the source of their power: because they cost so much time and effort to perform and yielded nothing practical, undergoing them was a costly signal that a member's commitment was genuine. What critics dismissed as waste was, on this reading, the institution's central mechanism.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It supplies historical detail about the specific manner in which the guild's rites were performed.
It concedes that the guild's rites were, exactly as their critics charged, entirely without value.
It introduces an objection that the final sentence then goes on to refute.
It advances an explanation on which an apparent defect turns out to serve a crucial function, an explanation the final sentence restates.

questions.passage: We tend to praise a perfect memory as an unalloyed good, but a mind that forgot nothing would be crippled. To think is largely to ignore—to treat this situation as sufficiently like that one to warrant the same response. A memory that preserved every particular in its full specificity would present no two situations as ever alike, and so would make impossible the generalization on which all reasoning depends. Forgetting is not memory's failure but the condition of thought.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Far from being a mere defect, forgetting makes possible the generalization that reasoning requires.
People who happen to have unusually good memories tend also to be the better reasoners.
The chief purpose of human memory is to preserve experiences in their full particularity.
Human reasoning would be greatly improved if only our memories were more nearly perfect.

questions.passage: She had imagined this morning a thousand times, and in every version of it she had wept for joy. Now she walked from empty room to empty room and felt only a curious flatness, as though the house, having been for so long the whole object of her wanting, had used itself up in being wanted, and had nothing left to give her now that the wanting was over.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Attaining the goal she had longed for leaves Odile strangely empty, the house having meant more to her as an object of desire than as a possession.
Odile is overjoyed at having finally reclaimed the house that had once belonged to her family.
Odile discovers that the house has fallen into serious disrepair during the years of her absence.
Odile comes to regret having spent so many years of her life saving to buy back the house.

questions.passage: The mantis shrimp's club-like forelimb strikes with such speed that it briefly boils the surrounding water, creating collapsing bubbles whose implosion produces a second shock wave. Prey that somehow survive the physical blow are often finished off by this cavitation pulse. Remarkably, the limb withstands thousands of such strikes without shattering, thanks to a layered internal architecture that channels any cracks harmlessly sideways rather than letting them run straight through.
questions.question: According to the text, what keeps the mantis shrimp's forelimb from shattering?
options: The collapsing bubbles that each of its strikes creates in the surrounding water.
A layered internal structure that redirects cracks sideways instead of letting them run straight through the limb.
The second shock wave that cavitation produces as the limb strikes its prey.
The extreme speed at which the forelimb moves during each of its strikes.

questions.passage: A literary scholar argues that an anonymous eighteenth-century pamphlet was written by a well-known statesman of the period rather than by the obscure printer whose name appears on it.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the scholar's argument?
options: The pamphlet repeatedly uses several unusual turns of phrase that appear, among all writers of the period, only in the statesman's signed correspondence.
The printer whose name appears on the pamphlet is known to have printed several other political pamphlets in the same year.
The pamphlet was widely read and went through five separate editions within a year of its first appearance.
The statesman is known to have publicly denied having had any involvement whatever with the pamphlet.

questions.passage: The memoirist Sela Roan is admired for registering grief obliquely, through a sudden swerve to the trivial rather than through direct statement. A critic illustrating this technique might quote the passage in which ______
questions.question: Which quotation from Roan's memoir most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “They told me my father had died in the night, and I was overcome by a grief that I have never since been able to put into words.”
“My father was, by any measure anyone might choose to apply, a difficult and often a distant man.”
“They told me my father had died in the night. I remember thinking, with great urgency, that the hallway clock would need winding, and that no one now knew how he had liked it set.”
“In the weeks that followed his death, the whole of the family gathered to settle his affairs.”

questions.passage: An economist argues that a city's 1990 ban on large billboards caused the subsequent rise in its downtown property values, reasoning that a less cluttered streetscape drew wealthier residents to the area.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken the economist's argument?
options: Residents surveyed after the ban reported finding the downtown streetscape considerably more attractive than before.
The billboard ban was opposed by several local advertising firms at the time it was first proposed.
Comparable cities that never banned billboards saw their downtown property values rise by the same amount over the same years.
Property values in the city's outer districts rose more slowly than those downtown in the years after the ban.

questions.passage: A geologist proposes that a large, smooth, rounded boulder resting far out on a flat plain was carried to its present spot by a glacier, not by a river.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the geologist's proposal?
options: The boulder's surface is smooth and rounded, much as the surfaces of boulders tumbled in fast rivers often become.
The boulder is of a rock type found only in mountains hundreds of kilometers away, across terrain that no river has ever crossed.
The plain on which the boulder rests receives heavy rainfall for much of the year.
Several smaller, sharply angular stones lie scattered in the soil immediately around the boulder.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • “Assortative mating” is the tendency of individuals to mate with others similar to themselves.
  • In humans, it has been observed for traits such as height and level of education.
  • Tall people, on average, tend to partner with taller people.
  • People with more education tend to partner with others of a similar education level.
  • Over generations, strong assortative mating can increase the variation in a trait across a population.
questions.question: The student wants to explain what assortative mating is to an audience unfamiliar with the term. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Over the course of generations, strong assortative mating can increase the variation in a trait across a population.

Assortative mating is the tendency of individuals to pair with others similar to themselves—in humans, for traits such as height and education, so that taller people, for instance, tend to partner with taller people.
In humans, assortative mating has been observed for such traits as height and level of education.
People with more education tend to partner with others who have a similar level of education.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The researcher Amina Farah hypothesized that, among bird species, those with more varied diets tend to have larger geographic ranges.
  • Species R eats 3 types of food; its range is 40,000 km2.
  • Species S eats 11 types of food; its range is 310,000 km2.
  • Species T eats 7 types of food; its range is 150,000 km2.
questions.question: The student wants to use the data to support Farah's hypothesis. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The species with the most varied diet, S (11 food types), had by far the largest range (310,000 km2), while the species with the least varied diet, R (3 food types), had the smallest (40,000 km2).
Species T eats 7 different types of food and has a geographic range of 150,000 km2.
All three of the bird species eat more than one single type of food.
Species S eats more types of food than both Species R and Species T.
